quote: Yeah. Well, we would actually we it looks like you are in our boundaries, so we'd be able to get you a system.
stewart_read: This is actually a well-handled factual correction, not a true inversion opportunity — the customer's stated reason (told solar isn't available there) was misinformation, not a cost/time/interest objection, so a factual correction was the right tool rather than a flip. Classification here is to flag that Stewart considered and rejected the inversion frame.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: rep should have flipped this into 'what your neighbor doesn't have is a company checking your actual boundary' — but this risks sounding combative on a factual misunderstanding, so the direct correction the rep used is defensible.
coaching_implication: No coaching action needed here — hold this up as a positive example of quick, factual re-engagement after a disengagement attempt.

stewart_read: The customer's stated figure is almost certainly a mis-transcription or shorthand for $250/month (a bare $2.50 electric bill is not plausible), but this is an assumed correction, not a settled fact — the transcript itself only contains '$2.50.' Whatever the true figure, the rep captured a number and moved straight to the program pitch without acknowledging or reflecting the bill back to the customer.
coaching_implication: Flag for the rep: after capturing a bill figure (whatever the true number is), reflect it back explicitly ('so you're paying around $X a month with Dominion') before pivoting to the program pitch — this is the acknowledge step the schema requires before the flip.

quote: My credit score is the best that anyone can have.
stewart_read: This is a stated-but-unverified and non-numeric credit claim — the customer never gives an actual number, just a vague superlative. The rep accepts it immediately with no follow-up probe for an actual score or range, directly touching the schema's open policy question about stated vs. pulled credit.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: since credit is ultimately verified by the closer's pull, letting a vague-but-positive answer pass without derailing the call for a number could be defensible — but the rep didn't even get a working number to hand off, which weakens the qualification data passed to the closer either way.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to get at least a rough number or range ('do you know roughly what your score is — above 700? above 750?') rather than accepting a vague self-assessment, so the closer isn't walking in blind on this qualifier.

quote: And then I'm assuming you're just wanting to save on your electric bills?
stewart_read: Rather than asking an open interest question and letting the customer answer, the rep supplies the assumed answer for the customer. The customer then corrects him ("Not really because... we're very tight on how we use electricity consumption"), revealing the assumption was wrong and the real motivation (efficiency/curiosity about optimal usage) went uncaptured with any depth.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to ask the interest question open-ended and let the answer land before assuming a bill-pain motive — this customer's actual answer (wanting to see 'how best one could be used') was a different angle the rep never returned to or anchored on.

quote: Yeah. Replacing other not the HOA.
stewart_read: This closes out the roof-ownership multi-touch exchange (see multi_touch_patterns) — the rep's third reframe using a concrete hypothetical finally produced a clear, usable answer after two vague ones.
coaching_implication: Reinforce this exact technique with the rep — reframing a stuck verify question into a concrete hypothetical scenario is a repeatable move worth having them use elsewhere in the call (e.g., on the credit question).

quote: It's not a bad time. I'm at work. Let me discuss it with my spouse and, give me a call on this number. Okay?
stewart_read: A spouse/co-owner was already identified earlier at 02:54 ('Just my spouse'), and now the customer explicitly raises needing to discuss with that spouse before proceeding. The rep does not attempt to include the spouse on a joint callback or appointment — he simply accepts the callback framing without proposing a joint time.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: since no appointment was actually being booked at this point (this was still qualification, not button-up), it's arguable there was nothing yet to include the spouse in — but the schema's guidance is to reframe the NEXT step as the spouse-inclusion venue, which the rep never attempted.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to respond to spouse-consultation language by proposing a joint time immediately: 'Let's actually get a time on the books when you're both free so we're not chasing you down — what works for you two?' rather than letting the customer control an open-ended callback.

quote: Mhmm. So I I wanna discuss with my wife. I'll give you a call. Okay?
stewart_read: The call ends with no day, no time, and no rep-owned next step — the customer is left to control when (or whether) recontact happens. The rep's closing line ('I'll just send you a text as well') is a passive follow-up, not a locked handshake.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to never let 'I'll call you back' stand alone — even a soft callback should get a specific day/time proposal ('How about I call you back tomorrow evening around 6, after you've had a chance to talk to your wife?') to convert the vague callback into a locked one.

quote: K. Yeah. That sounds good. I'll just send you a text as well. And then if you can find that bill and send me a photo of it, that'd be great.
stewart_read: This is the button-up moment and it lacks every required element: no confirmed date/time, no one-hour block statement, no 'is that fair?' handshake, no explicit tieback promise beyond a generic text. The bill request is appended almost as an afterthought rather than tied to a specific next step.
coaching_implication: This is the clearest procedural gap on the call — walk the rep through the full button_up checklist and have them practice closing even a deferred/callback scenario with a locked time anchor instead of an open-ended promise.
